embeddings.title: SoundMesh: Wireless Multi‑Point Audio
embeddings.description:
In studios, pop-up performances, and informal gatherings, distributing audio beyond one speaker often means long cable runs, fragile ad-hoc Bluetooth pairing, or expensive specialized systems. SoundMesh asks what a more legible and resilient approach could look like—one that a non-specialist can set up, and that still respects the realities of latency, dropouts, and room conditions.

The system uses transmitter and receiver nodes. A transmitter node connects to an audio source. Receiver nodes connect to speakers or headphones. Under the hood, nodes form a self-healing wireless network that maintains playback and adapts as nodes appear, disappear, or move. A companion portal visualizes topology and stream state so the network is not a black box, but something you can understand and tune.

embeddings.title: Generative Clothing; An Exploration
embeddings.description: Generative Clothing investigates what happens when the barrier to imagining and creating clothing is radically lowered — first through an AI pipeline that converts spoken descriptions into virtual garments, and then through modular fabric tiles that function as fundamental building blocks, giving anyone the means to visualize and physically construct their own clothing.

embeddings.title: You Have One New Voice message
embeddings.description:
You Have One New Voice Message is an interactive installation that inhabits the threshold between connection and longing with voicemail technology. The space a voice message occupies when a call goes unanswered, when connection falls just short of reach. Through landline telephones, you are invited to call, to listen, and to leave your own words behind. To reach towards something that was lost, a relationship, an identity, a time, or a place. 

Through the receiver, you are given a choice: to listen or to speak. 

To listen is to receive a stranger’s vulnerability, their words recorded before you arrived. 
To speak is to offer a personal story, a realization, a goodbye, trusting someone else will come after and hold it. The same spot, a different time, a different voice. 

Across these accumulated voices, you sit with what it means to be witnessed by someone you may never know. What lingers in another’s voice is not just the words left behind, but the relief of knowing that grief, longing, and the ache of distance is never entirely yours alone to carry. The installation asks you this question: what does it mean to hold space for a stranger’s words, and trust the silence enough to offer your own.

embeddings.title: Infrastructures of Distance, or the Logics of Thinning and Thickening
embeddings.description:
Infrastructures of Distance is a practice-based investigation into the social affordances of the internet. The project introduces two infrastructural conditions, Thinning and Thickening, as a framework for examining how internet-mediated communication shapes our interpersonal relationships. 
At the center of the work is the Fiber Navigator, a custom-built network visualization instrument that functions simultaneously as a home internet router and as a research device. By visualizing and recording network connections in real time, it seeks to render the normally invisible operations of internet infrastructure both perceptible and subject to scrutiny.

embeddings.title: Collected Exorcisms
embeddings.description:
Collected Exorcisms is poetry collection and art book developed through extended engagements with memory and loss. The book gathers 30 poetic vignettes with accompanying visual art blending handwritten notes, collage, performance, creative coding, montage, and 412 photographs from the author’s personal archive. Rather than beginning with a fixed structure, the work unfolded through an iterative, exploratory practice that involved returning to fragments, reworking them across multiple mediums, and allowing each version to shape the next. This process reflects how she has navigated grieving 11 different relationships through revisitation, rearrangement, and layering.

The final form of the printed book is a completed (‘closed’) piece, but emerged from a cyclical, often chaotic, workflow. To better convey the experience of processing, the author created a companion piece of web art, demonstrating how this concept can exist through a living medium, offering insight into the layers that sit beneath the finished poems and acknowledging that while the completed book may appear resolved, the path toward closure involves sustained, complex, and often non-linear work. Collected Exorcisms functions both as a record of grieving and as the outcome that emerges from it.

embeddings.title: Invisible Architecture
embeddings.description:
Research based speculation on what space becomes when the invisible wireless signals that surround us are made visible and navigable. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, radio, cellular networks, and other electromagnetic transmissions are usually hidden from sight, but they are constantly moving through the spaces we occupy. They pass through walls, objects, and bodies, shaping how we communicate, connect, and understand the built environment. This project asks what it would feel like to experience these invisible systems as a spatial layer of architecture.

The installation uses software defined radio, TouchDesigner, Arduino based sensing, and a custom handheld instrument to translate signal activity into a visual and interactive environment. Instead of decoding private information, the project treats signal behavior as material for abstraction. Broadcasts, interference, packets, pulses, and waves become lines, dashes, bars, and shifting geometries that move across a large visual field.

Viewers engage with the work through the handheld instrument. The controller allows them to move, aim, zoom, and search through the signal environment, turning the act of looking into a form of navigation. Through this interaction, the viewer does not simply observe the invisible layer; they physically explore it.

The project imagines the visual field as a section cut through space, revealing an infrastructure that already exists alongside the built environment. By making wireless activity visible and navigable, Invisible Architecture invites viewers to reconsider space as active, layered, and filled with unseen systems. The work is both technical and speculative, using sensing, visualization, and interaction to give form to the invisible conditions embedded in everyday life.

embeddings.title: Source Knowledge Nodes
embeddings.description:
Source Knowledge Nodes is a small network of jewelry-scale electronic devices that function as portable, human-curated libraries. Each charm, worn as a belt or charm, stores a deliberate collection of source materials: essays, PDFs, images, and the kind of pre-loved internet artifacts that shapes one's identity. Content lives on systems designed by ourselves, not on corporate servers. The project responds to a specific cultural moment: an internet increasingly saturated with AI-generated content, SEO-optimized noise, and platform-mediated knowledge. As generative AI floods the web with text that mimics authority without grounding, the original source materials that actually form human thought. The annotated essay, the scanned archive, the obscure reference is quietly disappearing. This project treats that disappearance as a design problem.

Each charm operates as a single-purpose device: it holds a small, carefully edited library, and shares it only through physical, proximate encounters. Two wearers who choose to exchange bring their nodes together - through touch, proximity, or gesture - and the devices trade selected materials in a brief, legible ritual signaled by light or haptics. There is no cloud intermediary. No algorithm decides what you receive. Only another person's curation does.

embeddings.title: Horizon
embeddings.description: Horizon is a spherical, immersive feedback system that places a 360° camera at the center of a 360° projection environment, collapsing capture and display into a single recursive loop. Rather than externalizing volumetric data onto an object, Horizon inverts the model: participants enter the sphere itself, surrounded by a live projection of the space they inhabit, rendered back to them in real time. The room becomes both camera and screen, a continuous boundary where presence is captured, processed, and reprojected onto the same surface from which it originates, producing an inside-out mirror of the immediate present.

embeddings.title: Interspace
embeddings.description:
Interspace is an AI-human collaborative drawing platform that challenges a fundamental assumption that AI should give us polished answers. 
Through user testing, I found that when AI produces finished images, exploration ends. Users stop asking questions. Their inherent creativity gets inhibited by polished results.

The project began with a hypothesis: what if unfinished forms could inspire more than finished images? My V1 used ASCII art with a chat interface, expecting that abstract representations would spark imagination. User testing broke that assumption. Users didn't need AI to generate ideas — they already knew what they wanted to draw. And similar images didn't inspire them; they just confirmed what they already had.
The insight was clear: users need expansion, not just confirmation.
This led to V2's dual-system solution, separating two distinct roles.
Echo reflects user intention through ASCII art. A quiet mirror that says "yes, that's your drawing" without trying to improve it. Imagine expands possibilities through AI-generated images that deliberately diverge from the original, asking "what about this possibility?" rather than "here's a better version."

The balance matters. When these roles operated in isolation, users felt either unseen (Imagine only) or stuck (Echo only). Together, Echo grounds the user's intention while Imagine opens unexpected doors.
Interspace reframes AI's role in creative work. It proposes that AI shouldn't provide ideas, it should reveal possibilities. The drawings created aren't the point; the transformed relationship between human intention and machine interpretation is.

embeddings.title: A Door Decorated by Stone
embeddings.description: This Mixed Reality installation reconstructs the sensory memory of a Shanghai Shikumen home. By combining a physical doorframe with off-axis projection and stereoscopic rendering, it creates an immersive, headset-free 3D environment. The project demonstrates how MR can preserve lived cultural memories, moving beyond static architectural symbols.

embeddings.title: The Machine
embeddings.description: The Machine is a web experience that explores the blurring of understanding between us and our machines. The bot watches you, listens, and responds through archival footage — old media mirroring our world.

embeddings.title: Kinly
embeddings.description:
Kinly is a care app designed to support older adults in a way that feels gentle, respectful, and human. Rather than focusing only on reminders or monitoring, this project explores how digital design can express emotional care and help people feel safe, connected, and independent.

This project is deeply influenced by my cultural background in Taiwan and my own first hand experience as a caregiver for a year. Through caregiving, I saw how support is often not only practical but emotional. Many older adults hesitate to accept help because they fear losing independence or becoming a burden to their families. In Taiwan and across East Asian cultures, dignity, family care, and emotional sensitivity shape how care is received. Kinly was designed in response to those values.

The app includes simple daily tools such as medication reminders, appointment tracking, and light health notes, but its focus goes beyond management. A shared family album allows loved ones to send daily photos, creating a quiet sense of presence. A gentle chat feature supports small moments of encouragement without feeling overwhelming. Light activities and learning tools offer calm engagement and support everyday wellbeing.

Every design decision aims to make care feel soft rather than clinical. Clear navigation, large touch areas, and a warm visual tone help older adults feel comfortable using the app on their own.

The project was also informed by real world conversations and testing with older adults in Taiwan, which helped shape the interaction design through lived feedback rather than assumptions.

Kinly is not just a care management tool, but a companion designed to support dignity, reduce emotional resistance to care, and help families stay connected in a more thoughtful way.

embeddings.title: Starling
embeddings.description: A proof assistant is a programming language and/or user interface that enables the creation of computer-aided proofs. Proof assistants are interactive theorem provers. Starling is a proof assistant designed for ease of use by novices.

embeddings.title: talk through me
embeddings.description: talk through me is a sound installation that interrogates the sound space inside each of us through archival material, sculpture, and spatial audio. the work uses an audio processing technique called convolution, which takes the spatial qualities of one audio and applies them to another. the first audio becomes space, the second goes inside that space. in this installation, i invite folks to explore my internal sound space, and put the different sounds that live inside my body into each another.

embeddings.title: Code name: baton
embeddings.description:
What if you could think like a photographer, paint like an illustrator, and design like a typographer — all at once?

Baton is a node-based, multi-creator AI canvas built on top of Doodlely — my sketch-first AI canvas where creators draw rough doodles instead of writing text prompts. Doodlely paired you with one creator persona at a time to iterate on your sketch. Baton picks up where Doodlely left off, turning that same canvas into a workflow where many personas work together.

Based on what you want to create, Baton generates a tailored team of creator personas and arranges their work as connected nodes on the canvas — A passes to B, B passes to C — like runners handing off a baton. A fashion designer might pass her sketch from fashion sketcher to technical designer to photographer. A chair lover might move from chair designer to photographer to illustrator. Each pass compounds the originality of the starting sketch.

Behind the scenes, an LLM-as-judge layer continuously evaluates how well each output matches the user's intent, refining accuracy across iterations. The result is a creative team that doesn't just respond to prompts — it reasons about them.

Baton is built for solo creators, independent artists, and small studios who need to move fast without sacrificing creative depth. Rather than replacing the creator's voice, it amplifies it, offering the range of a multidisciplinary team through the intimacy of a single canvas. The sketch-first interface lowers the barrier to entry, making advanced AI image generation accessible at every skill level.

I wish to suggest a new way of being a creator, asking you the only question that matters: What originality would you bring?

embeddings.title: Froth: A New Language for MCU's
embeddings.description:
Froth is a new programming language designed specifically for interactively programming microcontrollers. Inspired in Forth (a niche 70's phenomenon), Froth allows you to program, adapt, and change the behavior of running systems. It all happens in the MCU, meaning you can even program your device with something as dumb as a typewriter.


Froth is a project about usability, but also about hardware sustainability, openness, and resilience.

embeddings.title: Digital Aura
embeddings.description:
Digital Aura is an interactive installation that explores whether emotional authenticity can emerge from artificial systems. Centered on a series of AI-generated masks, the work does not seek to realistically replicate the human face. Instead, it expresses emotion through distortion, texture, light, and shifting form. Drawing from the visual language of ritual masks, speculative design, and machine-generated imagery, these masks move beyond fixed identity to become surfaces for carrying and transmitting feeling.

As viewers approach the installation, their presence and facial expressions influence the system, triggering real-time changes in the masks’ visual states. Calm, fear, grief, tension, and playfulness are translated into evolving synthetic faces that feel at once intimate and unfamiliar, blurring the boundary between human emotion and nonhuman form. Rather than asking whether AI can possess “real” emotion, the work considers how people project feeling onto artificial forms, and how digital images can still produce genuine emotional resonance.

Existing between sculpture, moving image, and responsive system, Digital Aura reconsiders the role of AI within contemporary image culture—not only as a tool for production, but as a medium for emotional speculation and reflection on authenticity.

embeddings.title: Laurel Blue: The Forms of Water
embeddings.description: Laurel Blue: The Forms of Water explores fashion as a living, responsive system by translating Gaston Bachelard’s six water imaginaries into a fashion tech & kinetic garment collection. Bridging traditional craftsmanship with innovative technologies such as 3D printing, laser cutting, and kinetic mechanisms, each piece transforms poetic states of water into embodied, oceanic experiences. Through experimental pattern-making, controlled tension systems, and soft-robotic structures, the garments move with and around the body, reflecting the fluidity and dynamism of the sea. Rather than treating clothing as static form, this work positions fashion as an interface for sensing and engaging with the environment, proposing a more attentive and coexistent relationship between humans and the ocean.

embeddings.title: Keep Refrigerated.
embeddings.description:
An interactive sculpture that frames milk as both artifact and system. The fridge holds six cartons across varied contexts: personal, nutritional, environmental, technological, political, historical. Each piece reworks the familiar carton form through felt, resin, metal, and newsprint, pushing the material and structural limits of the standard carton to carry their own narratives. Milk shifts from a mundane object into something that holds layered meaning.

Viewers engage directly by opening the fridge door and picking the cartons off the shelves.

embeddings.title: Echoes of the Gallop
embeddings.description: In this era of rapid digitalization—where everything can be recorded, stored, quantified as data, and modeled through computation—I seek through this work to explore how we might re-examine and redefine the partnership between humanity and nature. In this project, I use the partnership with horse in Chinese history to inspire the relationship with oysters in NYC.

embeddings.title: Veritas
embeddings.description:
The project is an art demo for a single-player roguelike action RPG, management hybrid game, focusing on environmental design and story-telling.

In a world scraped hollow by apocalypse, where survival is rationed and any spark of delight is a distant memory, a lone girl runs a questionable little shop from the dim shelter of her room. She sells Veritas—a fleeting rush of joy, a brief breath of something brighter than survival alone.

But her true supply lies deeper, hidden behind the soft hum of interdimensional portals blooming in the corners of her room. Beyond them stretch wondrous, perilous realms: labyrinths of strange beauty, ancient curiosities, and forbidden treasure. There, she becomes someone else entirely—an unbound warrior, fearless and relentless, gathering the veritas that keep her world tethered to its last traces of joy.

And yet the dual life pulls at her. The joy she trades and the freedom she tastes both vanish too quickly, slipping away like the shimmering dust she holds in her hands. As she ventures deeper into each world’s secrets, threads begin to intertwine—until she is forced to face a formidable choice.

The game extends the dual-gameplay loop framework by bringing about contrasting environments and conflicting settings in the two gameplay modes. Instead of keeping players immersed by designing two game modes that reinforce each other both mechanically and visually.

embeddings.title: 美怡+英菲
embeddings.description:
The title, 美怡+英菲, is a combination and mix of my grandma's and my own given names. The project explores narrative storytelling of two mirroring intergenerational stories, in particular, on how to leave room for speculation, regret, and imagination while respecting and commemorating someone’s history. How do we rewrite the sad endings of our loved ones without changing who they are and what they did? We project ourselves onto the story as we grieve, for it is such a personal thing: You do not grieve the “objective” person they were, but who they were to you and how they influenced you. The natural unreliable narrator we play as we grieve puts on a filter for them and distances us from our loved one in a way. 

Grief forces us to reflect upon ourselves as well. When you look back upon your linage, you recognize the similarity between yourself and your forebear and question whether you are destined to repeat their fate; you spot the differences and underline progress, only to doubt whether it is simply the changing current of times that pushed you forward and washed her to the shore, and would you have been able to check off the achievements if you were in her shoes? 

The project is dedicated to my late grandma, 美英, while shedding light on the subject of linage and willing vicariousness, the miscarried could’ve-been, and repetition in fate.

embeddings.title: The Room I Never Left
embeddings.description:
The Room I Never Left is a purely sonic, binaural spatial experience set in a dark room, tracing a queer woman’s search for self and her complex intimacy with her hometown. In this work, leaving is framed as both an act of self-discovery and an incomplete escape. The hometown and its memories become something she resists or fears returning to, yet they continue to shape her identity from afar.

The experience uses real-time motion capture to drive a responsive binaural sound environment within a confined square room, transforming the space into a landscape of dormant memories. Visitors are invited to navigate the dark room through sound. As they follow these sonic cues, their movement triggers intimate monologues and layered spatial soundscapes. The narration gradually unfolds as visitors uncover these fragments. Yet these sonic memories remain elusive, drawing visitors forward while staying just beyond reach, reflecting the experience of constantly returning to a past that cannot be fully touched.

The room becomes a spatial metaphor for the internal architecture of memory and identity. While the soundscapes evoke different times and places, the visitor’s body remains bound within the same four walls. The experience culminates in the realization that true departure never fully occurs, and that the past is not a place left behind, but an inseparable part of the self.

embeddings.title: SITU Search
embeddings.description: Manually cataloging thousands of hours of footage is slow, cumbersome, and often beyond the capacity of individual reporters, under-resourced newsrooms, and legal teams pursuing accountability. SITU Search meets this challenge. It builds on Codec, SITU's video management platform used by The Associated Press, The New York Times, Amnesty International, and Dutch law enforcement. Codec organizes visual evidence across time, space, and investigative priorities.. SITU Search extends this foundation with open-weight and proprietary machine learning models that automate consuming tasks such as detecting duplicates, clustering media, and cataloging events by time and location. Human editorial oversight is preserved throughout. The result transforms digital investigations  into a scalable, collaborative tool, enabling journalists, researchers, and lawyers to uncover human rights violations–from patterns of abusive policing to identifying weapons, locations, and other critical evidence.

embeddings.title: étape
embeddings.description:
étape is an interactive, multisensory virtual cycling experience built with Unreal Engine and Arduino-based physical computing. Participants’ steps on a mini-stepper will be captured by an ultrasonic sensor, which directly translates into the virtual avatar’s cycling speed and responsiveness, creating a synchronized embodied interaction between physical motion and the digital environment.

The project aims to express the joy of cycling through a handy mini-stepper. By integrating physical interactions with virtual feedback, the installation seeks to recreate the sensation of riding, turning an ordinary indoor workout into an immersive, interactive experience.

By merging embodied activity with audiovisual immersion, étape encourages users to discover the joy of cycling and, potentially, practice it in the real world on a real bike. Participants will have the chance to ride through dynamic landscapes and views inspired by real-life riding experiences, feeling the thrill of riding and the benefits of exercise.

embeddings.title: Umara: Songs of the Invisible
embeddings.description:
Umara is an immersive narrative-based interactive installation exploring social camouflage through deep-sea survival metaphors. Audiences follow a fictional creature’s story and use hand gestures to trigger visual responses, revealing different forms of hiding, adapting, and self-protection.

In this speculative underwater ecosystem, species survive by glowing to connect, mimicking to belong, and hiding to preserve themselves—behaviors that mirror how we navigate social overstimulation, miscommunication, and emotional exhaustion. The installation unfolds through a dual-projection system: a central narrative video is projected in front, while a secondary top-down mapping covers the floor and a pedestal-mounted coral statue, blurring the boundaries between the digital and the physical.

Participants interact with the ecosystem via a Leap Motion sensor hidden within the handcrafted coral sculpture. Through non-contact hand gestures, viewers influence the bioluminescent environment and the narrative flow. As a culmination of the journey, the system exports a personalized "Deep-Sea Persona Card" in real-time. This card maps the participant’s unique interaction data to a specific Umara species, providing a psychological reflection on their social camouflage patterns.

Merging fine craft with generative technology, UMARA serves as a reflective sanctuary. It questions how we might find more resilient and tender ways to perceive ourselves and connect with others when old modes of "hiding" or "shining" no longer suffice.

embeddings.title: Say My Names
embeddings.description:
In 2023, Columbia Journalism Review asked editors a simple question about trans coverage: "Whose voices are heard, and is anyone missing?"
I tried to answer that question with data. 

Media visibility is an important indicator for measuring the political status and cultural legitimacy of a social group. From 2016 to 2025, although the proportion of the LGBT+ community in the total population continued to rise, the distribution of media resources among the four core identities (Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Transgender) showed an extreme inversion and imbalance.

Say My Names is a data journalism visual essay built on 954,433 English-language U.S. online news articles from January 2016 through December 2025. It tracks four identity labels — gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender — measuring how much coverage each received, when that coverage spiked, and what kind of language surrounded each identity in the text.

embeddings.title: Parallel Hour
embeddings.description:
Parallel Hour is an interactive installation that explores how a simple physical gesture can reshape our perception of time and self.

By pulling a real string, users physically engage with a digital timeline rendered as a continuous red line representing the present moment. As the line is pulled, it begins to unravel, splitting into multiple parallel paths that suggest alternate versions of the same moment. These branching lines briefly coexist before collapsing, leaving a single remaining path—an imagined reality chosen from many possibilities.

Along this selected line, a short AI-generated text appears, describing what a parallel version of the user might be doing at that exact time. This moment transforms an abstract system into a personal and speculative reflection, connecting physical action with narrative imagination.

Combining tangible interaction, generative visuals, and real-time text, Parallel Hour invites users to reconsider the present not as a fixed state, but as one of many possible versions unfolding simultaneously.

embeddings.title: Rishta: Aunties Know Best
embeddings.description:
Rishta: Aunties Know Best is a social deduction board game in which players are all Aunties getting their collective daughter, Sara, married off. Sara thinks the most important thing is finding her perfect match. The Aunties know better. They have gathered to ensure Sara marries the perfect match for the family. Over the course of 4 rounds, players will share gossip about Sara’s suitors and arrange dates for her in order to meet their hidden agenda. If an Auntie succeeds in her agenda, then she wins the game. 
The game is authoethnographic; it draws on my experience as a South Asian Muslim daughter going through arranged dating experiences. The character of Sara has no voice in spite of being the focus of gameplay. It is intentionally designed to surface the unspoken expectations placed on daughters and the unconscious contradictions that arise from different understandings of tradition, culture, and family.

embeddings.title: Pulse of The Journey
embeddings.description: A pulsing music journey.

embeddings.title: GDJ - FV1
embeddings.description: The Guitar DJ Controller (GDJ) is a reimagining of the DJ interface as a fully embodied musical instrument. Combining the familiar form and ergonomics of a guitar with the functionality of a professional DJ controller, the GDJ transforms digital DJing into a visible, physical performance. Rather than standing behind a laptop or static controller, the performer holds, strums, and manipulates the instrument in space, making the act of mixing music legible and expressive to an audience.</br></br>The controller operates entirely through MIDI, making it compatible with any DJ or music production software while allowing complete customization of controls. Its wireless Bluetooth capability enables performers to move freely on stage, breaking away from the traditional fixed DJ setup. The neck of the instrument features a system of buttons that control stems, cues, loops, and effects, all activated through a strumming interaction that mirrors guitar playing. This design introduces a gestural language to DJing, where combinations of inputs can be performed rhythmically and physically.</br></br>Emerging from a broader cultural inquiry into the evolving nature of music, performance, and social connection, the GDJ addresses the growing disconnect between digital music manipulation and audience perception. By making the DJ’s actions tangible and performative, the project seeks to restore a sense of visibility, energy, and human presence to electronic music performance, reframing DJing as a live, expressive art form.

embeddings.title: NuMI
embeddings.description: Numi is a preventative health lifestyle management ecosystem that acts as a personalized lifestyle health coach, starting with reducing decision fatigue around what to eat throughout the day—especially while traveling or frequently on the move. The device would provide real-time, context-aware guidance based on available food options nearby, adapt to a user’s daily routines and circumstances, and support in-the-moment food and activity decisions while working quietly in the background.

embeddings.title: ColDAW: R&D of a Music Collab Framework
embeddings.description:
ColDAW is a collaborative music production platform that helps creators and teams keep project versions organized and collaborate across tools, so they spend less time managing files and more time creating. This thesis project is a series of research and development efforts examining the core of music production and its data logistics, with the goal of developing a creative solution to improve current workflows and provide better tooling for music creators.

Music creation has expanded rapidly alongside the broader rise of the creator economy and digital content production. Over 7 million people worldwide now use DAW software, yet the infrastructure supporting how creators work together has barely evolved. Music creators working across different software tools, locations, and timelines lack a structured way to organize, version, and collaborate on projects, with no industry-standard practices and widespread frustration around metadata, inconsistent formats, and broken version histories. The consequences are tangible. Creators waste hours rebuilding sessions and re-exporting audio files. For distributed teams working across different platforms, the pain is especially acute because these tools operate in closed ecosystems with no interoperability layer. 

ColDAW introduces a parsing and normalization pipeline that converts complex Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) sessions, including track hierarchies, clips, and automation, into a unified symbolic representation. The framework supports cross-tool interoperability, bridging DAWs with multimedia environments without requiring shared authoring tools.

embeddings.title: The Experimental Paint Archive
embeddings.description: The Experimental Paint Archive is a publicly accessible and open source collection of biodegradable, non-toxic, and reusable fine art materials. The history of paint is entwined with a history of material experimentation, and of people who have often taken considerable financial, physical, and environmental risks in order to attain specific visual effects. This project documents techniques through which the hazards associated with creating fine art materials from scratch can be minimized, and iterates upon the conventional pigment + binder + liquid vehicle formula.

embeddings.title: Memora - A Living Memory App
embeddings.description:
We store everything. We feel nothing.

Memora is a living memory companion — a mobile app that asks what digital remembering could feel like if it were designed around emotion, not efficiency. Most tools treat memory as data: folders, timestamps, archives. Memora treats it as something closer to what it actually is — a multisensory, emotionally charged reconstruction that shifts every time we return to it.

The project is grounded in cognitive memory research and multisensory HCI, drawing on studies of spatial recall, emotional encoding, and the psychology of closure. What the research consistently shows is that memory deepens when interfaces engage emotion, texture, and structure — not just storage. Memora is built around that insight.

The app organises memories by emotional quality — Joy, Calm, Love, Melancholy, Wonder, Nostalgia — rather than by date or category. A spatial Memory Map lets users navigate their past the way the mind actually does: through feeling and association, not chronology. A Mood Landscape visualises memories as orbiting emotional spheres. A Timeline traces the emotional arc of a life. And a Daily Reflection screen offers one quiet prompt each day, sealing the response and building an Emotional Weather portrait over time.

Every memory has a Closure Ritual — a meditative moment designed to help users process and honour an experience, not just log it. Memories can also be released entirely: a deliberate, irreversible act of letting go.

Memora challenges the assumption that digital tools should be neutral. It asks whether an interface can feel intimate without being intrusive, alive without being overwhelming, and human without being sentimental.

embeddings.title: to touch is to feel
embeddings.description:
to touch is to feel is a solo exhibition at The Living Gallery, Brooklyn, NY (April 9–13, 2026) examining immigrant labor, textile memory, and the technological histories embedded within craft traditions. 

Drawing from fabrics preserved from Brooklyn garment factories where my mother and aunt worked after immigrating to New York in the 1990s, I construct an interactive textile archive through artist books, soft sculpture, and projection installations. The exhibition connects sewing techniques such as pleating, embroidery, knitting, and crochet to computational systems, positioning feminized craft practices as early forms of programming and information encoding.

Activated through touch and proximity, the works invite viewers to physically engage with materials carrying histories of labor, migration, and survival. By bringing together textiles and electronics—two materials notoriously difficult to recycle—with the themes of human touch, memory, and earth, this project encourages us to reconnect with the tangible, affirming that technology’s origins are rooted in human craft and care.

Public programming throughout the exhibition included an artist talk, short film screening, poetry reading, and knitting workshop, expanding the exhibition into a space of collective learning and participation.

embeddings.title: The Seven Deadly Sins: Encore
embeddings.description:
Encore is a narrative roguelike deck-builder game set in a theater where the concept of an "ending" has collapsed. As a former ticket inspector, you must clear seven stages—each ruled by a "Sin"—by hitting a specific target score. 
In each round, a "Sin" gives you starting gold and demands specific Emotional Tags (e.g., Security, Connection). You use the shop to buy Event Cards, which represent fragments of life. You then play both Event Cards and Item Cards. Playing an Event Card causes an Item Card to drop. These Items are then added to your hand to be played for powerful combo effects. If the cards you play match the Sin’s requested tags, you earn bonus gold to further upgrade your deck. Your final score is the Product of your Event values and Item bonuses. Because the scoring is multiplicative, missing a single combo link can lead to failure. 
At the end of each stage, you must choose your development path: Encore Cards: Provide stability and help you repeat successful card sequences. Indulgence Cards: Offer massive, immediate power but carry a high cost. If you play four Indulgence cards, the system "Blackens." You enter a Lost State where all sophisticated Item combos are disabled. You are left with raw power, but you lose all narrative cohesion and strategic depth.

embeddings.title: Of Terrains We Speak
embeddings.description: How deep do we go to get to what we want to say? Do we wrap them in softer, cushioning words so that it reaches the listener more gently? What is it that we’re saying, and who are we saying it to? “Of Terrains We Speak” is a computational approach to visualize the latent ‘depths’ in conversations that we can feel but not see, in an attempt to find what it reveals about ourselves.

embeddings.title: Nido
embeddings.description:
This project, Nido, seeks to make 3D room design more accessible to people of all kinds, not just technical experts. There is a huge gap currently in how people engage with planning real 3D spaces. Either someone is a master user of an intricate and expensive 3D software, or they have to go off 2D information—photos and text—for a space. With the recent improvements in graphical compute and 3D capability on internet browsers through libraries like Three.js and SparkJS, we have the technical ability to close this gap but no cheap solutions currently.
        
Inspired by open source projects like Pascal and SuperSplat, I wanted to design a 3D scanning and receiving website that anyone could use. First, someone scans their room and objects with my iOS app. After processing the scans on the server, the results get read from the database to the website, where people can see their room with real dimensions in their browser.
        
Also on the browser, people can upload floorplans that become editable 3D structures using AI Agents, turn images of products into 3D objects with AI, and design iterations of their space with real measurements, without getting out a tape measure.

embeddings.title: Beetle Creator Studio
embeddings.description:
Approximately one out of every four known animal species on earth is a beetle. As the evolutionary biologist J.B.S Haldane put it “if one could conclude as to the nature of the Creator from a study of creation, it would appear that God has an inordinate fondness for beetles.” 


Beetle Creator Studio puts visitors in the role of an intern for the Creator of the Universe (metaphorically speaking), helping to meet the projected quota of 1-2 million species of beetles on Earth. 


Using a character-creator-style interface, visitors assemble a beetle by selecting from real morphological traits, each one illustrated with an actual example beetle species. While building, visitors can see what each adaptation suggests about how their beetle might compete, survive, and reproduce based on scientific research. They then release their beetle into a shared world and see it join the other previously created “species.” 


Through the act of making, I hope visitors leave Beetle Creator Studio with a little more appreciation for beetles and a deeper curiosity about evolution.

embeddings.title: The Tools That Bring Me Home
embeddings.description: "The Tools That Bring Me Home" is a set of two storytelling devices. Each device is an investigation of a personal history through the narrative of material culture and the medium of repurposed containers – a margarine container and five-gallon water jug. The containers are gateways to real experiences and memories that have the ability to transform unexpected findings into something to appreciate. They are the medium through which we act, understand ourselves and behaviors, and relate to one another.

embeddings.title: A Fermentation Jar for Small Bad Feelings
embeddings.description:
A Fermentation Jar for Small Bad Feelings is an interactive device that collects the small negative feelings that gather in everyday life and transforms them into a lightly humorous poem. Rather than focusing on major trauma or dramatic sadness, the project attends to micro-frustrations: awkward moments, minor disappointments, passing stress, and the quiet emotional residue of an ordinary day.

Inspired by the making of rice wine, the device takes the form of a fermentation jar. Throughout the day, the user carries a small portable recorder to collect these emotional fragments through short voice recordings. When placed on top of the jar, the recorder becomes its lid, sealing the container and beginning the transformation. The collected fragments are transcribed and appear inside the jar as words that fall in like raw ingredients, dissolve, release tiny bubbles, float and circulate, and gradually reorganize as they ferment. Ambient light gradually shifts from a cool tone to warm yellow, indicating that the fermentation is progressing and has reached maturity.

After this brief “fermentation,” the device returns the user’s own emotional fragments as a poem that is gentle, lightly humorous, imaginative, and emotionally supportive. The goal is not to erase unpleasant feelings, but to help users revisit them from a softer angle. Like fermentation itself, the original material remains, but its flavor changes. Because the poem is shaped through the user’s own participation and lived experience, it can feel more intimate and resonant.

embeddings.title: Time Map
embeddings.description: Time Map is an mobile app that share emotion and memory for users to experience digital and physical world.

embeddings.title: present
embeddings.description:
present is an interactive public installation that uses computer vision to detect human presence and project a fragment of light beside the person on a bench.
The installation consists of two everyday urban objects: a bench and a streetlight. A camera mounted on the streetlight monitors the bench in real time using a Python YOLO object detection model. When a person sits, the system extracts the bounding box coordinates of their body and projects light in that shape onto the bench surface beside them. The light remains as long as the person is present and disappears when they leave. No data is stored. No interaction is necessarily required.
The project departs from the conventional use of computer vision as a surveillance tool. CV(Computer Vision) technology was originally developed for military target identification and has since become the backbone of urban surveillance infrastructure — systems designed to classify, track, and modify human behavior. present redirects the same detection mechanism toward a different output: acknowledgment rather than control. The system does not identify who is sitting. It only registers that someone is there, and responds.
A bench and streetlight are infrastructure — objects embedded in daily urban life that they go unnoticed. By working within this register, the project asks whether CV can operate the same way: not as a marked artistic intervention, but as a quiet, persistent part of the city that simply notices the people who move through it.
present proposes that the same technology used to surveil can be redirected to acknowledge.

embeddings.title: Volta
embeddings.description:
Current is the most fundamental, and most misunderstood concept in DC circuits. Four decades of physics education research consistently show that students believe electricity gets "used up" as it travels through a circuit, that current flows only one way through components, and that batteries always push out the same amount of current no matter what. These misconceptions survive traditional classroom instruction largely unchanged, even at the graduate level.
Volta is a purpose-built educational device designed to make the invisible visible. A resistor inserted into the device immediately triggers a cascade of feedback: a wide bar display animates current flowing through the circuit in real time, LED strips along simulated wires pulse with directional movement, a bulb changes brightness in response to resistance, and a screen displays live Ohm's Law values voltage, resistance, and calculated current alongside the resistor's color code. Swap in a different resistor and every element of the display updates instantly.
The device runs on a LattePanda IOTA single-board computer with a built-in RP2040 co-processor handling all sensor measurement, LED animation, and hardware control. A FastAPI backend broadcasts live data via WebSocket to both displays simultaneously. The result is a compact, self-contained classroom tool that bridges the gap no existing tool has closed: the space between simulations that visualize current but cannot be handled, and physical circuits that can be handled but render current invisible.
Volta is designed for anyone curious about electricity

embeddings.title: Please CARE
embeddings.description: Please CARE is an interactive installation project about care labor: the invisible, uncompensated work of tending to something that needs you. A small entity lives on a dedicated screen. It waits. When you approach and touch it, the system registers your action as a unit output. When you leave, it accumulates debt. The entity does not pause, it is still here. The work exists as a physical object : a small screen running continuously waiting to be held. Care becomes spatial and material - the user must approach it, return to it and eventually abandon it. Neglect is not an abstract metric. It becomes a presence in the room. The system tracks care as measurable output. The entity responds in feeling. This gap between what the system demands and what care actually is, is the subject of this work.

embeddings.title: i see in you, what you see in a tree
embeddings.description: There is a lot we can learn from redwood trees- how to build resilience, community, and grow through hardship. I see in you, what you see in a tree is an interactive video art installation inspired by a poem written for my grandmother, and explores how the unique properties of redwood trees serve as symbols of the human experience. Just as the rings on a tree act as a natural record of moments and paint a picture of the tree’s growth, the tree rings of this piece tell a non-linear personal journey through sound and video activated by the intimate action of touch. By allowing others to reach out and ‘touch’ my stories, it is my hope to inspire others to reflect on their own experiences, find the courage to share with others, and consider how our lives are inextricably intertwined with the living beings that surround us. This piece is a testament to the power of finding yourself in dark places and growing through it while grappling with the complex feelings of both loss and joy that accompany transformative experiences. To learn more about the inspiration behind the project and the final piece, please visit the project's website linked at the top of the page.

embeddings.title: the soft computer
embeddings.description:
The Soft Computer is a textile-based computing object that imagines a gentler way of being with technology. Constructed from soft materials with machine-knit accents, it houses a flexible e-ink display, capacitive touch zones, a haptic motor, ambient sound, and breathing light, all enclosed in something you can hold in your lap.

It is designed to be sat with, not operated.

Four felt buttons act as a poetic keyboard, each one steering a generative text engine toward a different body of writing. A soft trackpad shifts the mood of the language. Poems accumulate slowly on the screen in response to touch, unhurried, material, present.

The Soft Computer draws on the long history of textiles and computing as entangled practices: the Jacquard loom as proto-program, the punch card as woven instruction. It asks what computing might look like if it inherited not just the logic of the loom but its texture, its slowness, its care.

This project proposes softness not as a limitation but as a design stance, against optimization, against command, against the assumption that faster and more efficient is always better. It is a speculative object and a functional one: a computer that generates poetry instead of productivity, that responds to presence instead of input.

What can a soft computer do that a hard computer never could? What becomes possible when we design computers around softness rather than hardness, around care rather than command?

embeddings.title: nabbing
embeddings.description:
nabbing is a Chrome extension that captures the transitory actions of copying and pasting. They are online behaviors so routine that they are often unnoticed, yet are still sufficient, at scale, to profile and redirect a person's attention.

The extension routes this data to a built-in factory where users process their own clipboard histories, categorizing each captured unit across three dimensions: intention, content, and mood. In the act of extraction, the original context collapses and only the categories remain. The factory's processing stations then attempt to make sense of these decontextualized fragments, producing reports, predictions, and profiles from information that is fundamentally incomplete.

As an extension of the project, nabbing is presented as a workshop: participants install the extension and use the browser normally for two weeks, then arrive for a "first day at work". They process their accumulated data in an office-like setting, whether in person or on Zoom, creating a shared experience of a "tool" that is otherwise private and solitary.

embeddings.title: Archival Mechanica
embeddings.description: Archival Mechanica is a portable archive that gives new home to obsolete personal devices. Drawing from traditions of storage, collection, and care, it offers these technologies a new place to reside after their functional lives have ended. The work explores how memory persists through the objects that accompany us over time.

embeddings.title: i'll love you as long as i know how
embeddings.description:
"i’ll love you as long as i know how" is a soft, collaborative sound sculpture that weaves together time-softened textiles, found materials, and an audience-responsive choral soundscape, encouraging audience-participants to move slowly, explore gently, and connect both literally and metaphorically with one another in the process. 

The heart of the piece exists in the interplay between three central entanglements: the materiality of the woven artifact, the collective resonance of the virtual choir, and the subtle shifts in audience-participants’ tempo and attention as they explore the piece together. When no one is nearby, the soundscape is silent and the lighting is dark; when multiple people interact simultaneously, these elements come to life. Underneath the inviting surface texture of well-loved textiles, custom-made capacitive touch sensors translate gentle touch into changes to both embedded lighting elements as well as in the ongoing soundscape. Fragmented from recordings of an original four-part vocal piece performed from dear friends from different creative chapters of my life and then further transformed through granular synthesis, the timbral clarity of each voice and breath rises and falls in direct response to audience-participants' interactions. Structure forms, dissolves, and forms again as people continue to engage.

Over and over again, audience-participants’ decisions to hold on or let go shape their individual and collective experience sonically, spatially, and emotionally as they navigate the piece together. In their hands, the sculpture becomes a portal for both sound and connection, a tactile reflection on and of how core truths of our relationships – platonic, romantic, familial, and otherwise – continue to resonate within us through the ebbs and flows of circumstance, proximity, and mutual understanding.

Special thanks to Addie Mathis, Ava Busler, Elian Carbone, and Octavio Figueroa Moya for contributing their voices to this piece, and to violet w-p for her input and guidance on the sound design.

A short demo of the piece can be found here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pL9ZVCRDTxA

embeddings.title: loose ends
embeddings.description:
This semi-autobiographical video game is about a knitter named Penny who finishes projects started by people who have died.

She’s just graduated from college, unemployed, and temporarily moves back into her childhood home. Her mom is away visiting her own mother, Penny’s grandmother, and so Penny is left to take care of the house and the cat.

During this monthlong period — June of 2009 — Penny begins volunteering for an organization that matches crafters like her with the loved ones of people who have passed away or otherwise left projects unfinished. By completing these assignments, the player learns more about who these strangers were, and is gradually exposed to Penny’s own relationship to grief after the death of a friend.

The volunteer organization is based on the real-life work of a nonprofit called The Loose Ends Project, also the namesake of the game, which has successfully matched finishers with over five thousand completed projects to date.

The game can be played in any browser (desktop preferred), as well as on the hand-knitted arcade console created for its presentation. It’s meant to convey warmth, tactility, and intimacy, even and especially in the face of loss.

embeddings.title: Data + Emotion
embeddings.description:
Data and emotion seem like they are on the opposite ends of the spectrum. Data has an impression of being cold-hard truth, and emotion is a highly subjective feeling. But that’s not always the case. Data is often being collected by someone with certain goals and subjective biases, and emotion is often an objective means to spark action. For the longest time, communication of data prioritised efficiency. In doing so, we confine ourselves to the same visual structures and rob audiences of a deeper level of engagement. 

We can begin to break free from this by asking what happens when we think of data-viz as a medium of expression instead of a tool for analysis. I’ve started to see such sparks from influential data-viz practitioners, and my goal is to engage and contribute to the discourse. This sensibility is certainly not appropriate in all contexts, and there are pitfalls of manipulation and weaponization of data where emotion is involved. Which is why I believe having these conversations are important.

At its core this is a website, an archive if you will, to get an understanding of expressive data visualization, asking how and where it has its place in the communication of information. It’s put together via a collection of conversations with people in the industry, those who practice data-viz day in and day out, accompanied by my own thoughts and sketches conceived from these conversations.

embeddings.title: www.jujubewire.com
embeddings.description: www.jujubewire.com is an ongoing mixed media collage series exploring migration, identity, and memory. Each act of movement creates a new identity, while the previous one begins to fade. Through layered digital and physical fragments, the work traces how memories decay, distort, and reorganize over time, never fully disappearing, but never staying whole.

embeddings.title: VisiPronounce
embeddings.description:
VisiPronounce is an AI-powered pronunciation learning tool that helps users improve spoken language through real-time visual feedback. Unlike most language-learning apps that focus mainly on audio examples, VisiPronounce addresses a key challenge in pronunciation: learners often do not know how to position their mouth correctly to produce a sound.

By combining mouth-shape detection with pronunciation analysis, the project offers more personalized and actionable guidance on articulation. Instead of simply telling users whether a sound is right or wrong, it helps them understand how to adjust their lips or mouth shape to improve.

This project explores how AI and visual interaction can make pronunciation learning more intuitive, embodied, and effective.

embeddings.title: Everything I've Let Go of Has Claw Marks on It
embeddings.description:
Everything I’ve Let Go of Has Claw Marks on It is a kinetic installation that explores what it means to want wholeheartedly, often to one’s own detriment. An autonomous claw machine performs choreographed movements that echo human longing. The viewer becomes a bystander to its visceral struggle as it reaches endlessly toward a set of keys, representing access to a person, an opportunity, or a life just out of reach.

Stripped of coins and any possibility of reward, the machine no longer offers play, only persistence. The work asks what it means to be built for wanting in a world where access is never guaranteed.

embeddings.title: Lingering Lines
embeddings.description: ‘Lingering Lines’ is an interactive installation that explores how human emotions linger within spaces. Inspired by the intimate yet isolated nature of a public phone booth, participants speak into a receiver, and their emotions are translated into haptic and light-based expressions. These emotional traces are not experienced immediately, but are passed on to the next visitor, creating a delayed connection between strangers. Through this temporal exchange, the work invites reflection on presence, absence, and the invisible emotional residues we leave behind.

embeddings.title: Guan
embeddings.description:
Guan is an interactive installation that dissolves the boundary between the digital and the physical through the act of looking.
A digital ice block waits on the screen. As viewers hold their gaze, it melts — releasing real water droplets into the world. Attention becomes transformation. Observation becomes erosion.
To watch is to act. To see is to change what is seen.

embeddings.title: The Period God
embeddings.description:
The Period God “姨妈神” is a social practice project inspired by a vernacular internet deity in China, an imagined figure believed to govern menstruation.This project explores the cultural stigma surrounding menstruation and transforms private experiences into a shared public conversation.
For the installation, participants kneel before a screen in a traditional posture of reverence, yet the interaction subverts religious hierarchy. Touching the digital shrine triggers a physical red fountain, revealing the deity not as a feared idol, but as an equal mirror reflecting the horizontal solidarity of the female experience.

embeddings.title: What Remains...
embeddings.description: What Remains... is an interactive installation built from Hsiao's own digital history — images, text, and data that accumulate in real time, layering without resolution. Nothing is deleted. Each trace compounds the last, until individual presence becomes indistinguishable from the system that holds it.

embeddings.title: Hypnagogia
embeddings.description:
Hypnagogia is a ritual of yearning for places that may never have existed. The work explores memory as fabrication, childhood memories shaped by trauma and desire, composite pasts hovering between truth and imagination.
The work examines longing for homes that cannot be found, where the dream of a place becomes indistinguishable from the place itself. Reality and fantasy dissolve into each other, as familiar and ungraspable as a home you almost remember, where every act of remembering is also an act of forgetting.

embeddings.title: Hoomps (Previously Conquer), Social Media for making habit with friends
embeddings.description: Hoomps is a social platform focusing on creating good healthy habits with others, making doing a good habit fun while also having social layer for the credibility, it's social first rather than tracking first, so people could share their progress by themselves or with others

embeddings.title: ¿te quedas para el lonche?
embeddings.description:
Rooted in the Peruvian tradition of an evening merienda, the work invites audiences into a space of informal gathering and participation.

At its center, a crocheted tablecloth becomes a living, responsive surface, animated through projection and the movement of surrounding bodies, as their physical energy accumulates and is shared. This real-time interaction grounds the audience in the present, while familiar household objects and recorded home audio evoke traces of tradition, memory, and the past.

The installation considers how we inhabit shared space: how rituals of togetherness change over time, and how much remains the same.

embeddings.title: Block Party
embeddings.description:
Block Party is an interactive installation that transforms physical creation into a living digital character.

Participants sit at a table with a Lite-Brite peg board and a palette of colored pegs, building whatever they want. When ready, a document scanner mounted above captures their creation and sends it through an AI pipeline powered by Gemini AI.

The result appears on a high-resolution TV monitor beside the table — a sprite that walks, emotes, and exists alongside every character that came before it in a digital neighborhood.

After the experience, participants can revisit their creation through a shared web gallery where every sprite lives as its own collectible card — showing the creator's name and the sprite's unique traits, alongside everyone else's creations, and yours to save and keep. The gallery grows with every new participant, becoming its own kind of neighborhood.

At its core, Block Party explores what happens to our creations as they travel across forms. It is an open invitation for children and adults alike to make something, to wonder how much of themselves made it through, and to experience a moment of joy, delight, and play.

embeddings.title: Rhizo: A Martian Architecture Movement
embeddings.description:
Over the past few years, I have witnessed an era of deep societal fragmentation. I believe space exploration remains a powerful way to unite humanity.

Rhizo is a vertical Mars habitat located 150 meters deep within the lava tubes of Elysium Planitia. Designed as a living prototype for planetary exploration, the structure is under 10 meters of Martian regolith. Furthermore, a radiotrophic fungi wall system, effectively blocks lethal radiation and stabilizes extreme thermal fluctuations.

The habitat accommodates approximately 350 residents within a closed-loop ecosystem. By integrating vertical greenhouses with advanced air and water recycling systems, Rhizo ensures both physical survival and psychological well-being. More than just a shelter, Rhizo represents a vision of humanity taking root in the cosmos, reawakening the collective spirit that once defined the first moon landing.

embeddings.title: Floating Umbrella
embeddings.description:
Floating Umbrella is a hands-free umbrella that asks what rain protection could become if it no longer had to be held. The project grew from a simple experience. A friend and I were caught in heavy rain while carrying things, and the inconvenience of using an umbrella with full hands made me rethink the object itself. Why does such a common tool still depend on one free hand and constant adjustment?
This project proposes an umbrella that moves with its user instead of being carried by them. Floating Umbrella is designed to follow a single person and remain overhead while they walk, stop, or change direction, offering personal cover without direct manual control.
The project sits between interaction design and personal robotics. I am interested in how a familiar object changes when it becomes mobile and responsive, and how that shift affects a person’s sense of comfort, attention, and space.
As a prototype, Floating Umbrella responds to a practical problem while also asking a broader question. What happens when an everyday object stops being something we hold and becomes something that accompanies us?

embeddings.title: De Light
embeddings.description:
De Light is a dynamic natural light installation that transforms everyday sunlight into a quiet, immersive experience. Using reflective and refractive materials, the work captures and redirects sunlight into shifting caustic patterns that unfold across interior surfaces. Positioned by the window, a wooden structure resembling ordinary interior furniture subtly shapes how light enters and disperses into the space.

Rather than producing its own illumination, the installation relies entirely on ambient daylight, allowing the work to evolve continuously with time, weather, and season. As visitors move through the space, their presence triggers subtle mechanical movements that alter the angle and tension of reflective surfaces. These shifts interrupt and reshape the light, casting shadows and momentarily transforming the patterns. In this way, the installation becomes a shared environment where light, material, and human movement co-create the visual experience.

Inspired by fleeting moments of reflection and refraction in urban life—glints on windows, ripples of light on walls—De Light amplifies these often overlooked phenomena. The work encourages a shift in attention from the fast pace of daily life to the present moment, offering a brief release and a quiet moment of delight.

embeddings.title: Seed
embeddings.description:
Seed DuD is an AI-powered family history curation tool that transforms personal family materials—photographs, oral histories, objects, and documents—into exhibition-quality curatorial writing about a family member.
Rather than asserting biographical facts, Seed DuD builds the world around a person, drawing on archival and historical sources to situate them within their time, place, and culture. The project is grounded in a principle of epistemic care: it distinguishes between documented facts, contextual generalizations, and individual inferences, keeping the work honest about the boundary between what is known and what is imagined.
The result reframes family history not as a record to be asserted, but as memory given a frame to resonate against.

embeddings.title: Inner View
embeddings.description: Inner View is designed to reflect and visualize the unseen aspects of the surrounding space. By guiding our attention inward, the work invites us to detach from the chaos and noise of the external world, creating a space for meditation and reflection on the internal rhythms that shape our lives.Using sensors attached to the ground surface, it detects vibrations from the below, representing the constant and often unnoticed fluctuations of the external world. These vibrations activate subtle transformations in the installation’s form and generate deep metallic sounds and digital animation, creating an immersive and meditative atmosphere.

embeddings.title: Kanik
embeddings.description:
Kanik is an interactive installation where visitors knead and squeeze a ball of conductive dough to trigger fragmented audiovisual memories on a screen next to the installation. The project maps a deeply personal experience: playing with dough in my grandmother's kitchen in India while she cooked for the family, onto a tactile interface that anyone can engage with.

The installation uses an Arduino-based capacitive sensing circuit embedded in salt-based conductive dough. When a visitor touches or squeezes the dough, the varying resistance triggers different layers of audiovisual content through TouchDesigner - gentle contact surfaces a video of compiled memories: a tiny kitchen with square tiles, sounds of mustard seeds popping in oil, a pressure cooker going off every few minutes, a faint radio in the distance, cats on the walls outside, crows on the wires

The interaction is intuitive and you don't read instructions. You just touch, the way a child does. The project argues that  tactile interaction with culturally resonant materials can bypass language and access embodied memory.

embeddings.title: Wave Shaper
embeddings.description:
How does the cabinet design of a loudspeaker affect the sonic performance of a speaker? Wave Shaper is a speaker cabinet design that allows the user to explore the relationship between sonic reproduction and the physical structure that shapes it. The current design of Wave Shaper enables swift, tool-free adjustments to the critical structures within the speaker cabinet, facilitating sonic exploration and fostering an intuitive understanding of how each element contributes to the final sound.
Using an aluminum extrusion skeleton instead of adhesives to permanently fix the cabinet, this speaker also serves as a foundation for rapid integration and experimentation with custom physical designs, allowing users to immediately listen to the resulting effects. Given the unconventional use of hardware not typically designed for speaker bodies, extensive materials research was conducted for this project, which will be available online along with the build plans for the cabinet itself. This is an evolving project that aims to encourage the user to experiment with their own cabinet variations and contribute to a growing, shared understanding of how physical structure shapes sound.

embeddings.title: A Moment In Time
embeddings.description: A Moment In Time is a singular VR experience where viewer will enter into photorealistic environments to explore narratives inside this space. There are moments where thoughts does not always translate into spoken words and this experience captures that moment in time where the user has the liberty to explore this duality between the inner thoughts and the spoken words. In the virtual world, there will be characters placed in the scene, and as the viewer approaches one of them, a short re-enactment of a scene will play. They will get to witness relatable and familiar scenarios that they often face, and with a press of a button, the viewer will be able to listen into their inner thoughts and hear what these characters are truly thinking about.

embeddings.title: EVOLVING PORTRAIT
embeddings.description:
EVOLVING PORTRAIT is a social experiment in a form of a generative photobooth inspired by the CAPTCHA system, that visualizes the audience's inputs as an ever-evolving face. It takes a picture of you and blends your face with the archive of all the past users, and eventually makes a single evolving portrait. It's a data visualization project in a format of a face, using AI diffusion models and a question that prompts users.

Try the project: evolvingportrait.me

embeddings.title: Hairy Subject
embeddings.description:
Hairy Subject is an ongoing research project surveying hair waste’s material poetics as a metaphor of lineage, selfhood, and female labor.

It consists of:
1. Untitled: a jigsaw puzzle made of artist's collected hair, resin, and mirror acrylic
2. Matrilineal Hair Archive: 
- a 2 day interactive installation crowdsourcing hair + a trait that is passed down from said participant's maternal side
- a book of the installation's crowdsourced results
- a web archive of the installation's crowdsourced results
3. Hairy Subject (Digital Gallery)
- a web-base gallery of hairy artwork curated from the artist's research process

embeddings.title: Alluvial
embeddings.description:
Alluvial is a ceramic light installation that reveals hidden space until light finds its way through.

The exterior is made with textured clay, while the inside features a metallic glaze that fractures the embedded light into shifting reflections, exposing the geometry of the hollow shapes.

Drawing from the layered logic of the natural world, Alluvial brings together organic clay and embedded electronics, allowing light and matter to shape one another.

embeddings.title: Cube
embeddings.description: From a single cube expressed in 3 dimensional space to generative to actuation system, making an artistic practice from intuitive spatial understanding to motion and behavior study, reaching the State of the Art human visual reasoning with a cube. What can be achieve without direct representation from visual intuitions

embeddings.title: Team Stamps
embeddings.description:
Team Stamps is a webapp built for an amateur basketball league.
It enables the league's statskeeper to create and deliver interactive stats to teams.
The product aims to gamify statskeeping and amplify human interaction in team sports.

embeddings.title: People I Hate
embeddings.description: People I Hate is a three-book thesis project that begins with family tension and ends in self-definition. I am the illegitimate daughter in my family. I did not choose that position, but I live inside it. I have two older stepsisters, and although we are placed in similar roles, we are not treated the same. My dad likes me more. He brings me to events, introduces me to people, and openly says I am his best daughter. Naturally, they hate me. I hate them too. This project does not ask for pity, healing, or moral approval. It is not about forgiveness. It is about saying something clearly. The first book is direct and aggressive. I reduce my stepsisters to surface and insult, joking about their appearance and personality. Hate, at its simplest, is reduction. The second book turns hate into repetition and structure. It contains 180 bad wishes and 180 statements of denial: everything they want, they do not get—I get it. This book shifts from insult to position, showing that what they want already belongs to me. The third book removes them completely. It becomes a celebration of myself—my talent, my intelligence, and the life I built. I realized the reason I occupy this position is not only family structure, but also because I am capable, disciplined, and talented. The three books use my iPhone, iPad, and MacBook as covers, inviting viewers into my personal devices: my phone holds the images, my iPad holds the lists, and my MacBook holds my work.

embeddings.title: The Secret Ingredient
embeddings.description:
Gossiping, one of the oldest technologies to exist, is something we constantly do but rarely talk about. This project talks about it.

The Secret Ingredient is a web-based gossip lab, exploring the parallels between gossip and technology through the metaphor of a kitchen, where the tea gets spilled, the pot gets stirred, the dirt gets dished and the juice gets squeezed. The masala gets added! Gossip borrows a lot of its vocabulary from kitchens.

Gossip and kitchens share a long history: both are feminized and trivialized, but hold communities together. The word gossip itself comes from godsibb, once the warm shorthand for the women who gathered around births and deaths and dinner tables. Somewhere along the way, that gathering got renamed a sin. This project is an attempt at reclaiming it.

Today, gossip lives in our screenshots, voice notes and group chats. The Secret Ingredient follows it through the technologies we swore we'd use responsibly and asks what it would look like to design for the intimacy gossip actually needs.

From a secret ingredient to a recipe for community. Gossip is a tool.

embeddings.title: Lumenar series
embeddings.description:
LUMENAR SERIES is a light-based interactive series rooted in the artist's own experience of nyctophobia. Before they had bodies, these beings existed only as light. When they came down to earth, each took on a physical form drawn from a different source of light in the artist's life.
Lumemaru drew its form from the Korean Buddhist stone lantern (석등) — a guardian that has stood for centuries, radiating light to protect all who come before it. It reads the light reflected from the human body through a camera, and delivers its response as a blessing, spoken entirely in a custom light language in which every word is assigned a specific color.
Luminaru took on a form shaped by the first light the artist remembers — a plug-in mosquito repellent diffuser, small enough to exist right beside you. It receives and interprets sound through a microphone, and delivers its response as a blessing, spoken in the same language of light.
More details and video: www.jiyou-park.works

embeddings.title: Recho
embeddings.description: Recho is a free, open-source, reactive programming interface for algorithms and ASCII art. It introduces a plain code format for notebooks — echoing output inline as comments for live, in-situ coding with instant feedback.
